entries.meaning: A formal leather shoe worn with a suit or with office clothes. ---
examples: He polished his dress shoes the night before the interview.
You can't wear sneakers to a wedding, so bring a dress shoe or two.
Her dress shoes were killing her by the end of the reception.

entries.meaning: A light, cushioned athletic shoe made for running. ---
examples: I replace my running shoes every five hundred miles.
A good running shoe should feel snug in the heel.
She bought her first pair of real running shoes before the marathon.

entries.meaning: A soft canvas or leather sports shoe with a rubber sole. ---
examples: Grandma calls every sneaker a tennis shoe.
The kids tracked mud in with their tennis shoes.
Wear tennis shoes to the museum — there's a lot of walking.
entries.contrast: In much of the US tennis shoes means sneakers of any kind, not just shoes for tennis. British English says trainers.

entries.meaning: Any shoe designed for sports or exercise. ---
examples: The store's whole back wall is athletic shoes.
Gym class requires a closed-toe athletic shoe.
Athletic shoes have gotten a lot more expensive.
entries.contrast: Athletic has three syllables: ath-LET-ik. Adding a fourth ("ath-uh-LET-ik") is a common mistake.

entries.meaning: A high-cut athletic shoe that supports the ankle on the court. ---
examples: He saved up all summer for those basketball shoes.
A basketball shoe needs grip and ankle support.
The team gets new basketball shoes every season.

entries.meaning: A sturdy, comfortable shoe made for walking long distances. ---
examples: Pack one pair of walking shoes for the trip.
A cushioned walking shoe saved my knees.
These walking shoes look plain but they're wonderful.

entries.meaning: A woman's shoe with a tall heel that raises the back of the foot. ---
examples: She kicked off her high heels under the table.
I can barely walk in a high heel that tall.
High heels aren't allowed on the boat deck.

entries.meaning: A stiff boot with a deep-tread sole for walking on rough ground. ---
examples: Break in your hiking boots before the trip.
One hiking boot is still caked in dried mud.
Good hiking boots keep your ankles from rolling.

entries.meaning: A heavy protective boot worn on a job site. ---
examples: He left his muddy work boots on the porch.
The company pays for one pair of work boots a year.
A steel-toe work boot is required on this site.

entries.meaning: A tall leather boot with a pointed toe and a slanted heel. ---
examples: He wore cowboy boots to his own wedding.
That cowboy boot has hand-stitching all up the shaft.
Her cowboy boots click on the hardwood floor.

entries.meaning: A waterproof rubber boot worn in wet weather. ---
examples: The kids splashed through puddles in their rain boots.
I keep a rain boot by each door in the spring.
Yellow rain boots are easy to spot in a crowd of children.
entries.contrast: American rain boots are British wellingtons or wellies.

entries.meaning: A tall insulated boot that keeps snow and cold out. ---
examples: Put your snow boots on before you go outside.
One snow boot is missing from the closet again.
Her snow boots are lined with fleece.

entries.meaning: A warm boot made for cold weather. ---
examples: I finally bought winter boots that actually stay dry.
A good winter boot is worth the money in Minnesota.
The store puts winter boots on sale every February.

entries.meaning: A short boot that ends just above the ankle. ---
examples: She wears black ankle boots with everything.
This ankle boot has a side zipper.
Ankle boots work with jeans or a dress.

entries.meaning: A boot whose shaft reaches the knee. ---
examples: She pulled on her knee-high boots over her jeans.
A knee-high boot has to fit your calf, not just your foot.
Brown knee-high boots go with almost any coat.
entries.contrast: The k in knee is silent: nee-HY.

entries.meaning: A boot that comes up over the knee to the thigh. ---
examples: Thigh-high boots came back in style that winter.
She wore a thigh-high boot in the fashion show.
Those thigh-high boots are hard to walk in.

entries.meaning: A tall laced military boot with a thick sole. ---
examples: He still wears his old combat boots to work in the yard.
A combat boot takes forever to lace up.
Black combat boots were everywhere at the concert.
entries.contrast: The noun combat stresses the first syllable, KAHM-bat; the verb stresses the second, kum-BAT.

entries.meaning: A rigid plastic boot that clamps into a ski binding. ---
examples: Ski boots are miserable to walk in.
He loosened one ski boot on the lift.
Rental ski boots never quite fit right.

entries.meaning: A tall smooth-soled boot worn for horseback riding. ---
examples: Her riding boots are polished before every lesson.
A riding boot has a low heel that won't slip through the stirrup.
He keeps his riding boots in the tack room.

entries.meaning: A boot with a rubber bottom and a leather upper, worn in slush. ---
examples: Everyone on campus wears duck boots in March.
A duck boot handles wet snow better than a sneaker.
My duck boots are twenty years old and still dry.

entries.meaning: A low suede ankle boot with two eyelets and a crepe sole. ---
examples: Sand-colored desert boots go with jeans or chinos.
He's had that desert boot resoled twice.
Desert boots are comfortable right out of the box.
entries.contrast: Desert (DEZ-urt, dry land) is not dessert (dih-ZURT, the sweet course).

entries.meaning: A plain ankle boot with two or three pairs of eyelets. ---
examples: He wears brown chukkas to the office on Fridays.
A leather chukka dresses up a pair of jeans.
These chukkas have a rubber sole instead of crepe.

entries.meaning: A short boot ending at the ankle, or a soft knitted shoe for a baby. ---
examples: She paired suede booties with a wool skirt.
Grandma knitted a tiny bootie for each foot.
Those booties have a two-inch block heel.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like booty (treasure, or slang for the backside); only the spelling separates them.

entries.meaning: Waterproof rubber overshoes pulled on over ordinary shoes. ---
examples: He pulled galoshes over his loafers before heading out.
A pair of galoshes lives in the hall closet.
Her galoshes squeaked on the tile floor.
entries.contrast: Used only in the plural: a pair of galoshes, never "a galosh."

entries.meaning: A rubber shoe worn over a regular shoe to keep it dry. ---
examples: The mail carrier wears overshoes all winter.
Slip an overshoe on before you cross the lot.
Overshoes keep the salt off good leather.

entries.meaning: A wide flat frame strapped to a boot so you can walk on deep snow. ---
examples: We rented snowshoes at the ranger station.
One snowshoe came loose halfway up the hill.
Snowshoes spread your weight so you don't sink.

entries.meaning: Waterproof boots joined to trousers, worn for standing in water. ---
examples: He stepped into the river in chest waders.
My waders sprang a leak at the knee.
A pair of waders hangs in the garage all summer.
entries.contrast: Always plural, like pants: a pair of waders.

entries.meaning: A soft shoe worn only indoors. ---
examples: He shuffled to the kitchen in his house shoes.
Leave one house shoe by each side of the bed.
My grandmother never wore anything but house shoes at home.

entries.meaning: A backless shoe with a thick wooden or cork sole. ---
examples: Nurses on that floor all wear clogs.
She slipped a clog off under the desk.
Wooden clogs are loud on a tile floor.

entries.meaning: A soft flat leather shoe with the sole wrapped up and stitched to the top. ---
examples: He drives in a pair of old moccasins.
The stitching on that moccasin is done by hand.
Deerskin moccasins are soft as socks.

entries.meaning: A low dress shoe whose lace flaps are stitched closed at the bottom. ---
examples: Black oxfords are the safest choice with a dark suit.
He had one oxford resoled and the other polished.
Those brown oxfords need new laces.

entries.meaning: A slip-on shoe with a leather strap across the top with a small slot in it. ---
examples: He wore penny loafers with no socks all summer.
There's still a dime tucked in one penny loafer.
Her penny loafers were part of the school uniform.

entries.meaning: A leather slip-on with a white non-marking sole, made for wet decks. ---
examples: Boat shoes have grooves cut into the sole for grip.
He keeps one boat shoe on the dock as a doorstop.
Everyone at the marina wears boat shoes.

entries.meaning: A casual summer shoe with a canvas upper and a braided rope sole. ---
examples: She wore white espadrilles to the beach wedding.
The rope on one espadrille is starting to fray.
Espadrilles fall apart if you get them wet.
entries.contrast: French spelling, English sound: the final e is silent — es-puh-DRIL.

entries.meaning: A soft flat women's shoe shaped like a dancer's slipper. ---
examples: She keeps ballet flats in her bag for the walk home.
A ballet flat offers almost no arch support.
Black ballet flats go with everything in her closet.
entries.contrast: Ballet ends in a silent t and is stressed on the second syllable: ba-LAY.

entries.meaning: A flat sandal held on by many straps running up the ankle. ---
examples: Gladiator sandals leave funny tan lines.
One strap on her gladiator sandal snapped.
She bought brown gladiator sandals for the trip to Greece.

entries.meaning: A very thin, very high heel, or a shoe with one. ---
examples: Her stilettos sank into the wet grass.
A four-inch stiletto is not made for cobblestones.
Stilettos can dent a hardwood floor.

entries.meaning: A short, slim heel about two inches high. ---
examples: She wore kitten heels to the office all week.
A kitten heel is far easier to stand in all day.
Those kitten heels look dressy without being painful.

entries.meaning: A wide, square heel that gives a shoe more stability. ---
examples: These boots have a chunky block heel.
Block heels are much easier to walk in than stilettos.
She picked the sandal with the block heel for the wedding.

entries.meaning: A heel that runs in one solid piece from the back of the shoe to the toe. ---
examples: A wedge heel spreads your weight better than a thin one.
Her cork wedge heels are perfect for summer.
The sandals come with a low wedge heel.

entries.meaning: A shoe with a thick sole under the whole foot that adds height. ---
examples: Platform shoes came back in style again.
That platform shoe adds three inches.
She danced all night in white platform shoes.

entries.meaning: A shoe that is open at the back with a strap around the heel. ---
examples: She wore navy slingbacks to the luncheon.
The buckle on my slingback keeps coming undone.
Slingbacks are cooler than closed pumps in July.

entries.meaning: A shoe with a small opening that shows the tips of the toes. ---
examples: She chose ivory peep-toes for the ceremony.
A peep-toe means you need a pedicure.
Those peep-toes are surprisingly comfortable.

entries.meaning: A shoe with no laces that you push your foot straight into. ---
examples: Slip-ons are great for the airport security line.
He wears a canvas slip-on around the house.
Her black slip-ons pass for dress shoes.
entries.contrast: The noun stresses the first word, SLIP-ahn; the verb phrase slip on stresses the second: "just slip ON your shoes."

entries.meaning: A shoe or boot fastened with laces. ---
examples: He prefers lace-ups to loafers for work.
A tall lace-up takes a minute to get into.
These leather lace-ups will last for years.
entries.contrast: As a noun it is written with a hyphen and stressed on lace; the verb is two words: "lace up your boots."

entries.meaning: A sneaker cut high enough to cover the ankle. ---
examples: He laced up his red high-tops.
A canvas high-top is a classic look.
High-tops give your ankle a little more support.

entries.meaning: A sneaker cut below the ankle. ---
examples: He owns the same sneaker in low-top and high-top.
Low-tops are cooler in the summer.
She wears white low-tops with everything.

entries.meaning: A dress shoe with a pointed leather cap shaped like wings across the toe. ---
examples: He wore brown wingtips with a gray suit.
The perforations on a wingtip are purely decorative.
Those wingtips have been in his closet for a decade.

entries.meaning: A sturdy leather shoe decorated with rows of punched holes. ---
examples: He bought a pair of tan brogues for the spring.
The pattern on that brogue is beautiful.
Brogues look good with tweed.
entries.contrast: The same word also means a strong regional accent, especially an Irish one: "he spoke with a soft brogue."

entries.meaning: A white lace-up shoe with a band of dark leather across the middle. ---
examples: The dance team wore black-and-white saddle shoes.
That saddle shoe looks straight out of 1955.
Saddle shoes were part of the school uniform.

entries.meaning: A work shoe built to protect the foot from injury. ---
examples: The plant requires safety shoes on the floor.
A safety shoe has a reinforced toe and a slip-resistant sole.
They give every new hire a voucher for safety shoes.

entries.meaning: A metal cap built into the front of a work boot to protect the toes. ---
examples: These boots have a steel toe and cost twice as much.
The steel toe saved his foot when the pipe rolled off.
Boots with steel toes set off the metal detector.
entries.contrast: Steel sounds exactly like steal; only the spelling tells them apart.

entries.meaning: A light mesh-and-rubber shoe worn in lakes, rivers, or the ocean. ---
examples: Wear water shoes — the rocks are sharp.
A water shoe drains and dries in minutes.
The kids' water shoes are still in the car.

entries.meaning: A dance shoe with metal plates screwed to the toe and heel. ---
examples: You can hear her tap shoes from the parking lot.
The screws on one tap shoe worked loose.
Tap shoes are not allowed on the gym floor.

entries.meaning: A stiff satin ballet shoe that lets a dancer stand on the tips of her toes. ---
examples: She sews the ribbons onto every pair of pointe shoes herself.
A pointe shoe lasts a serious dancer only a few weeks.
The company orders pointe shoes by the case.
entries.contrast: Pointe is French but sounds exactly like point; the e is silent.

entries.meaning: A flat rental shoe with a smooth sole that lets you slide on the lane. ---
examples: We had to rent bowling shoes at the counter.
Every bowling shoe has the size printed on the heel.
Those red-and-blue bowling shoes are hideous.

entries.meaning: A tight rubber-soled shoe worn for rock climbing. ---
examples: Climbing shoes are supposed to feel too small.
He takes one climbing shoe off between routes.
The gym rents climbing shoes for five dollars.
entries.contrast: The b in climbing is silent: KLY-ming.

entries.meaning: A stiff-soled shoe that clips onto a bicycle pedal. ---
examples: His cycling shoes click across the coffee shop floor.
A cycling shoe has a cleat bolted to the sole.
Cycling shoes are useless for walking.

entries.meaning: A flat, heavily padded sneaker made to grip a skateboard. ---
examples: He wears through a pair of skate shoes every two months.
A skate shoe has a flat vulcanized sole.
Those skate shoes have double stitching at the toe.

entries.meaning: A shoe with gripping studs in the sole, worn on a golf course. ---
examples: He changed into his golf shoes in the parking lot.
A modern golf shoe uses plastic spikes, not metal.
Golf shoes aren't allowed in the clubhouse.

entries.meaning: A short metal point screwed into the sole of a track or golf shoe. ---
examples: She laced up her spikes for the 400.
You can replace a worn spike with a small wrench.
Metal spikes tear up the turf.

entries.meaning: A shoe built to correct or relieve a problem with the foot. ---
examples: Her doctor prescribed orthopedic shoes.
An orthopedic shoe is wider through the toe box.
Insurance covered one pair of orthopedic shoes a year.

entries.meaning: A shoe with a hidden lift inside that makes the wearer look taller. ---
examples: The actor wore elevator shoes in every scene with her.
An elevator shoe can add two or three inches.
You'd never guess those were elevator shoes.

entries.meaning: The bottom layer of a shoe, the part that touches the ground. ---
examples: The rubber outsole is glued and stitched on.
Check the outsole for even wear.
Both outsoles are worn smooth at the heel.

entries.meaning: The layer inside a shoe that the bottom of the foot rests on. ---
examples: Pull the insole out and let it dry overnight.
New insoles made these boots comfortable again.
The insole had flattened out completely.

entries.meaning: The soft cushioning layer between the outsole and the foot. ---
examples: The foam midsole breaks down long before the tread does.
Runners replace shoes when the midsole goes flat.
These midsoles are made of two different foams.

entries.meaning: The shaped surface inside a shoe that supports the whole foot. ---
examples: The cork footbed molds to your foot over time.
These sandals have a contoured footbed.
Both footbeds are removable and washable.

entries.meaning: The whole part of a shoe above the sole. ---
examples: The upper is one piece of full-grain leather.
Water gets in where the upper meets the sole.
The soles were fine, but both uppers had cracked.

entries.meaning: The front part of a shoe's upper, covering the toes and instep. ---
examples: The vamp is stitched to the quarters at the seam.
A low vamp shows more of the foot.
The vamps on both shoes had creased deeply.
entries.contrast: The same spelling also means a seductive woman, or a short repeated passage in music.

entries.meaning: The rounded front section of a shoe where the toes sit. ---
examples: My little toe rubs against the toe box.
Look for a wide toe box if you have bunions.
The toe boxes on these boots are reinforced.

entries.meaning: A separate piece of leather or metal over the front of a shoe. ---
examples: The toe cap is scuffed but the rest is fine.
A rubber toe cap keeps the boot from wearing through.
Both toe caps took a beating on the trail.

entries.meaning: The stiff piece inside the back of a shoe that holds the heel in place. ---
examples: A firm heel counter keeps your foot from sliding around.
The heel counter collapsed after two seasons.
Cheap sneakers have soft heel counters.

entries.meaning: A hollow in an insole that cradles the heel. ---
examples: The deep heel cup keeps my foot centered.
He wears a gel heel cup for his heel pain.
These insoles have molded heel cups.

entries.meaning: A wedge put inside a shoe to raise one heel. ---
examples: One leg is shorter, so he wears a heel lift.
The podiatrist added a quarter-inch heel lift.
Heel lifts are cheap and easy to swap out.

entries.meaning: The small replaceable piece on the very bottom of a heel. ---
examples: The heel caps wore off and now the nails are showing.
A cobbler can put on a new heel cap in ten minutes.
The rubber heel cap came off on the escalator.

entries.meaning: How far a shoe raises the back of the foot off the ground. ---
examples: The listing gives a heel height of three inches.
She's fine with any heel height under two inches.
The same style comes in three heel heights.

entries.meaning: A strip of leather stitched between the upper and the sole of a shoe. ---
examples: A shoe with a welt can be resoled many times.
The stitching along the welt had rotted.
Both welts were replaced during the rebuild.
entries.contrast: The same word also means a raised red mark on the skin from a blow.

entries.meaning: The little plastic or metal tip on the end of a shoelace. ---
examples: The aglet came off and now the lace won't go through.
You can make a new aglet with a piece of tape.
Both aglets had split down the middle.

entries.meaning: The arched top of the foot between the toes and the ankle. ---
examples: The strap sits right across my instep.
He has a high instep, so most loafers pinch.
The laces left marks on both insteps.

entries.meaning: A thick rubber sole with deep blocks cut into it for grip. ---
examples: The lug sole grips wet rock well.
Boots with a lug sole pick up a lot of mud.
Lug soles are heavy but they last.

entries.meaning: A shoe bottom made of rubber, valued for grip and wear. ---
examples: The rubber sole squeaks on the gym floor.
He had rubber soles put on his dress shoes for winter.
A rubber sole is safer on ice than leather.

entries.meaning: A shoe bottom made of stiff leather, typical of dress shoes. ---
examples: A leather sole is slippery until it's broken in.
Leather soles wear out fast on concrete.
The shoes have a leather sole with a rubber heel.

entries.meaning: A soft, springy sole made of natural crinkled rubber. ---
examples: Desert boots usually come with a crepe sole.
A crepe sole is quiet but it picks up every bit of grit.
Crepe soles get sticky on hot pavement.
entries.contrast: Spelled like the thin pancake, and here pronounced the same way: KRAYP.

entries.meaning: The thin removable layer that sits directly under the foot in a sneaker. ---
examples: Take the sock liner out to wash it.
A worn sock liner is easy and cheap to replace.
Both sock liners had curled at the toe.

entries.meaning: A shaped piece in or added to a shoe that holds up the arch of the foot. ---
examples: These sandals have real arch support.
He slipped an arch support into each boot.
Arch supports helped my back more than anything else.

entries.meaning: A custom insole made to correct the way a foot sits or moves. ---
examples: Her orthotics were molded from a cast of her feet.
He moves one orthotic from shoe to shoe.
Custom orthotics are expensive but they lasted years.

entries.meaning: A pad or insole you buy separately and slide into a shoe. ---
examples: Gel shoe inserts made the standing bearable.
He picked up a shoe insert at the drugstore.
The shoe inserts come in one size and you trim them.
entries.contrast: The noun insert stresses the first syllable, IN-surt; the verb stresses the second, in-SURT.

entries.meaning: The tall part of a boot that covers the leg above the ankle. ---
examples: The boot shaft is too narrow for my calf.
She tucked her jeans into the boot shaft.
The boot shafts had cracked from being folded down.

entries.meaning: A removable felt or foam inner boot that adds warmth. ---
examples: Pull the boot liners out to dry by the fire.
A wet boot liner takes all night to dry.
The boot liners on his old pack boots are shot.

entries.meaning: A long, heavy lace for a boot. ---
examples: He snapped a bootlace pulling it tight.
Waxed bootlaces hold a knot better.
I keep spare bootlaces in my pack.

entries.meaning: A small open metal hook on a boot that a lace catches on. ---
examples: The top lace hook bent out of shape.
Boots with lace hooks are much faster to put on.
The lace slipped off the lace hook again.

entries.meaning: A metal ring set into a lace hole to keep it from tearing. ---
examples: One grommet pulled clean out of the leather.
Brass grommets look good on work boots.
The grommets are rusted but the boots are fine.

entries.meaning: A loop at the top of a boot that you pull on to get the boot over your foot. ---
examples: He grabbed both bootstraps and yanked.
The bootstrap tore right off the leather.
Tall boots usually have a bootstrap on each side.
entries.contrast: The idiom "pull yourself up by your bootstraps" (succeed with no help) is far more common than the literal loop.

entries.meaning: A band around the ankle that holds a shoe or sandal on the foot. ---
examples: The ankle strap buckles on the outside.
Ankle straps can make your legs look shorter.
The ankle strap rubbed a blister by noon.

entries.meaning: The way laces are threaded through a shoe. ---
examples: Loosen the lacing over the instep and the pinching stops.
The lacing on these boots crosses over the tongue.
There's a trick to lacing that keeps your heel from slipping.

entries.meaning: The grip a sole has on the ground. ---
examples: These soles have terrible traction on wet tile.
Winter boots need traction on ice, not just warmth.
The deep tread gives you good traction in mud.

entries.meaning: The soft material in a shoe that absorbs the shock of each step. ---
examples: There's almost no cushioning left in these sneakers.
The new model added cushioning under the heel.
Nurses want cushioning more than anything else.

entries.meaning: How wide a shoe is made, shown by a letter after the size. ---
examples: This brand comes in three shoe widths.
He needs a wide shoe width because of his bunions.
Shoe width matters as much as length.

entries.meaning: Leather with a hard, shiny coating on the surface. ---
examples: Her patent leather pumps caught the light.
Patent leather scuffs easily and can't be polished out.
He wore black patent leather shoes with his tuxedo.
entries.contrast: Americans say PAT-nt leather; the British say PAY-tnt. The US patent office is PAT-nt too.

entries.meaning: Leather sanded on the outside to give it a soft, velvety surface. ---
examples: The boots are nubuck, so keep them out of the rain.
Nubuck marks if you so much as touch it with a wet hand.
A nubuck upper needs a special brush.

entries.meaning: Fine soft leather from a young cow, used for good dress shoes. ---
examples: The uppers are smooth calfskin.
Calfskin takes a polish beautifully.
These gloves and shoes are both calfskin.
entries.contrast: The l in calf is silent: KAF-skin.

entries.meaning: Thick, tough leather from an adult cow. ---
examples: The work boots are heavy cowhide.
Cowhide is stiff at first but softens with wear.
He bought a whole side of cowhide for the shop.

entries.meaning: Leather with its natural outer surface left on, the strongest kind. ---
examples: These boots use full-grain leather throughout.
Full-grain leather develops a patina over the years.
You pay more for full-grain leather, and it shows.

entries.meaning: A plastic material made to look like leather. ---
examples: The boots are faux leather, which is why they're forty dollars.
Faux leather cracks after a couple of winters.
She only buys faux leather shoes.
entries.contrast: Faux is French: it rhymes with go, and the x is silent.

entries.meaning: Waxy paste or cream rubbed on leather shoes to color and shine them. ---
examples: He got shoe polish all over the kitchen towel.
We're out of black shoe polish.
A tin of shoe polish lasts for years.

entries.meaning: A cleaning and polishing of someone's shoes. ---
examples: He got a shoeshine in the airport terminal.
A good shoeshine costs eight dollars downtown.
The stand does about forty shoeshines a day.

entries.meaning: A stiff-bristled brush for cleaning or buffing shoes. ---
examples: Knock the dried mud off with a shoe brush.
He keeps a shoe brush in the hall closet.
Use separate shoe brushes for black and brown.

entries.meaning: A soft rag used to rub a shine onto leather. ---
examples: Wrap the polishing cloth tight around two fingers.
An old T-shirt makes a fine polishing cloth.
The polishing cloths are black with old wax.

entries.meaning: A soft conditioner rubbed into leather to keep it from drying out. ---
examples: Work the leather cream in with your fingers.
Leather cream feeds the leather; wax just shines it.
He puts leather cream on his boots twice a year.

entries.meaning: A mild soap made for cleaning leather without drying it. ---
examples: Clean the salt stains off with saddle soap.
A can of saddle soap costs a few dollars.
Use saddle soap first, then polish.

entries.meaning: A treatment that keeps water from soaking into a shoe. ---
examples: The waterproofing wears off after a season.
Spray waterproofing on before the first snow.
These boots come with waterproofing built in.

entries.meaning: Rubbing polished leather with a cloth or brush to bring up a shine. ---
examples: A little buffing and they look new.
The shine comes from the buffing, not the polish.
Buffing by hand takes longer but works better.

entries.meaning: Replacing the worn-out sole of a shoe with a new one. ---
examples: Resoling costs about sixty dollars a pair.
These boots are worth resoling.
The shop does resoling in about a week.

entries.meaning: A mark on leather where the surface has been rubbed or scraped. ---
examples: There's a scuff on the toe of my left shoe.
Polish hides most small scuffs.
The subway stairs put a deep scuff in the heel.

entries.meaning: The trade of fixing worn or damaged shoes. ---
examples: There's a shoe repair place next to the dry cleaner.
Shoe repair is cheaper than buying new boots.
He's been in shoe repair for thirty years.

entries.meaning: Someone who makes shoes by hand. ---
examples: A shoemaker in the village made boots to order.
The shoemaker measured both of his feet.
There are only a few shoemakers left in the city.

entries.meaning: The craft of making shoes. ---
examples: He learned shoemaking from his father.
Shoemaking used to be done entirely by hand.
The school offers a course in shoemaking.

entries.meaning: The foot-shaped wooden or plastic form that a shoe is built around. ---
examples: Every brand builds its shoes on a different last.
The shop carved a wooden last for each customer.
Two shoes on the same last will fit the same way.
entries.contrast: Spelled and said like last meaning 'final,' but this is a separate noun from shoemaking.

entries.meaning: A foot-shaped form put inside a shoe to hold its shape while it is stored. ---
examples: Cedar shoe trees pull the moisture out overnight.
Put a shoe tree in as soon as you take them off.
He has shoe trees in every pair he owns.

entries.meaning: A curved piece of metal or plastic that helps your heel slide into a shoe. ---
examples: There's a long shoehorn hanging by the door.
Use a shoehorn and you won't crush the heel counter.
The store keeps shoehorns at every bench.

entries.meaning: A tool cranked open inside a shoe to widen it. ---
examples: The cobbler left them on a shoe stretcher overnight.
A shoe stretcher can gain you half a size.
Shoe stretchers only work on leather.

entries.meaning: A notched board you step on to pull a tight boot off. ---
examples: There's a bootjack on the back porch.
Use the bootjack — don't drag mud through the house.
Old bootjacks are shaped like a beetle.

entries.meaning: A device that blows warm air into wet boots to dry them. ---
examples: The ski lodge has a boot dryer in the mudroom.
A boot dryer saves your boots from smelling.
We ran both pairs on the boot dryer overnight.

entries.meaning: A stand or shelf for storing shoes in rows. ---
examples: Please put your sneakers on the shoe rack.
We bought a shoe rack for the entryway.
The closet has two shoe racks on the floor.

entries.meaning: The part of a large store where footwear is sold. ---
examples: The shoe department is on the second floor.
She worked in the shoe department one summer.
Both shoe departments were having a sale.

entries.meaning: The number that says how long a person's foot or a shoe is. ---
examples: What's your shoe size?
My shoe size went up after I had kids.
American and European shoe sizes don't match.

entries.meaning: A shoe size halfway between two whole numbers. ---
examples: Go up a half size if you'll wear thick socks.
This brand doesn't make half sizes.
A half size is about a sixth of an inch.
entries.contrast: The l in half is silent: HAF.

entries.meaning: A thin slip-on cover that keeps a shoe clean or keeps dirt off a floor. ---
examples: The plumber pulled on blue shoe covers at the door.
Each visitor gets a paper shoe cover for each foot.
The clinic hands out shoe covers at the entrance.

entries.meaning: A cover strapped over a boot and lower leg to keep out snow or brush. ---
examples: Put your gaiters on before the snow gets deep.
One gaiter came unbuckled on the descent.
Gaiters keep gravel out of your boots.
entries.contrast: Sounds almost exactly like gator (alligator) in American speech.

entries.meaning: A thin nylon garment covering the feet, legs, and hips in one piece. ---
examples: Her pantyhose ran on the way to the interview.
She keeps a spare pair of pantyhose in her desk.
Nobody wears pantyhose to the office anymore.
entries.contrast: Never counted with a number — say a pair of pantyhose, and use a plural verb: "my pantyhose are torn." The British say tights.

entries.meaning: A sock that comes up to the middle of the calf. ---
examples: He buys white crew socks by the twelve-pack.
A crew sock sits just below the calf.
Crew socks are back in style with sneakers.

entries.meaning: A short sock that ends at the ankle. ---
examples: She wears ankle socks with her running shoes.
One ankle sock always disappears in the dryer.
Ankle socks are cooler in the summer.

entries.meaning: A long sock reaching up to the knee. ---
examples: The uniform includes navy knee socks.
She pulled one knee sock up over her calf.
Knee socks keep your legs warm under boots.
entries.contrast: The k in knee is silent: NEE sock.

entries.meaning: A very low sock that stays hidden inside the shoe. ---
examples: He wears no-show socks with his loafers.
A no-show sock slides off my heel every time.
No-show socks need a grip strip in the back.

entries.meaning: A thin sock worn with dress shoes and a suit. ---
examples: Pack two pairs of black dress socks.
A thin dress sock won't take up room in the shoe.
His dress socks had a subtle pattern.

entries.meaning: A thick cushioned sock worn for sports. ---
examples: Bring clean athletic socks to practice.
An athletic sock has extra padding at the heel.
The team hands out athletic socks on the first day.

entries.meaning: A thick tall sock worn inside boots. ---
examples: Wool boot socks are worth every penny in January.
A wet boot sock will give you blisters fast.
He packed three pairs of boot socks for the trip.

entries.meaning: A tight sock that squeezes the leg to help the blood move. ---
examples: She wears compression socks on long flights.
A compression sock is a fight to get on.
The doctor recommended compression socks after surgery.

entries.meaning: A new piece of sole put on the front part of a shoe only. ---
examples: The cobbler put a half sole on both shoes.
A half sole costs half what a full resole does.
Rubber half soles add grip to leather shoes.

entries.meaning: A flat backless sandal with one wide band across the foot.
examples: He wears slides to the pool and nowhere else.
One slide floated off down the lake.
Rubber slides dry in about a minute.
entries.contrast: The same word also means a playground slide or a photographic slide; the sandal sense is nearly always plural.
